decision.audit_notes: Verified current-session dialogue; decision evidence remapped to cleaned source.

evidence.text: I think you answered everything perfectly. And I love the hustle and the scrappiness. Of course, you've done a lot with very little. I also think that there is a big opportunity here. The valuation for me is really pricey, to be honest. Like this is where we come in with Hustle Fund. Um. For that reason I'm a pass. If you want to do revenue based financing, that is something we can potentially discuss.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: I’m Jaclyn. I’m the cofounder and CEO of Pepper. Who in here has ever felt self-conscious about any part of their body?

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I have!

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Okay. So sounds like everyone in this room. Well 91% of women who wear small cup sizes say at one point they wish their bust was bigger. And this is because we live in a world where, at a young age, girls already feel the pressure to develop during puberty. In middle school, they’re teased for being flat. As an adult, they walk into the biggest retailer of bras in the mall and are humiliated when a sales associate gives them a push-up bra to look two sizes bigger. And bras never seem to fit. These women deal with awkward cup gaps from not being able to fill in the cups all the way because they’re too deep. Or they have to deal with unnatural bulky pushup padding. This was my experience and the experience of so many other women that we found, and is what inspired us to create Pepper.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: We make bras that finally fit and celebrate women with small cup sizes. Turns out this is a $5.1 billion industry that’s anything but small. Since we went live, our Kickstarter campaign was 100% funded in the first ten hours. Since our official launch last year, we’ve already grown 8x. And this year we’re making $3 million in revenue run rate. I’m here today...

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Damn.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: ...to raise 1.5 million to grow our community and expand even faster with more products.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Congrats.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: That’s amazing.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Great!

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Do you know what the terms of the round are?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yes. So we’re doing a $9 million cap. Let me show this to you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Have a box of, I think, 3 bras. It looks like a pretty normal bra. It’s got a wire frame. Some pretty good padding with lace.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: What is it about your bras that makes them fit better?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Cos I'm like looking at it and it's not immediately obvious to me how, how…

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: So the number one pain point we were solving for is cup gap. And when we looked at why this was, traditional bar companies design for a 36C. That is what they think the industry standard is. So the first thing we had to do was develop our own cup molds. We used a cup mold that’s a shallower in depth. So it’s easier to fill for these women. So for these bras that you see here, we have three styles right now. And what makes them special is that you’ll notice there is a demi cup and a layer of mesh that goes on top. So this kind of has the effect of the perfect pair of yoga pants. It’s able to lift from the bottom up, really scooping you up in a natural way so you get really nice lift, even without that bulky push-up padding.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I feel like I'm also in this, this demographic. Um, but I usually don't wear a bra. Kind of because. Right? It’s like, I mean...

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Yeah. I very often go braless.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: That’s it, yeah, right, like that’s the thing is like I feel like I don’t really need like support or whatever.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And what do you sell these for?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: It ranges from $48 to $54.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: And what are your margins in the product?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: 71%. And this includes the end fulfilment to the customer.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Got it.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: How do you find your customer?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: So we have a few theories about who those segments are. Um, so we know that bra size and bust size has a lot to do with genetics. For example, I'm Asian American. A lot of women, similar to me, have very similar bust size. So we'll target that way. And we'll feature Asian American models, for example. Women who finish breast feeding tell us they used to be a C cup, now they're a AA cup. And they found our bras because they were looking for something that now fits their body as it is today. Another community that we recently just discovered who loves our products are transgender women. So during the transitioning process, you know, their bodies are also changing really quickly and they're trying to find a brand that not only fits them but speaks directly to them.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And so if you are using paid acquisition, what does that look like right now?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: So we’re doing Facebook ads and Instagram ads. We’re also diving into Google AdWords right now, um, which has been amazing because women are constantly searching for a solution to this pain point.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: What do they search for?

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I know. What words?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yeah, they’ll search for things really specific. Like, best bras for 34 AA.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Best bras for, best bras for 38 AA. It’s very specific. And because a lot of other companies aren’t really focusing on this size range, we’re just capturing all that traffic.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: What about just overall CAC?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yeah. So overall CAC is $25. And our lifetime value is $130. And we expect this lifetime value to go even higher, because right now we only have three products, we want to increase that.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Okay. So if you plan on raising a tranche of capital to pour into paid acquisition, roughly how much are you thinking that might be? Or how much would be interesting?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Well, out of the $1.5 million, we're thinking about doing um $1 million that goes towards paid acquisition.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Oh wow.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yeah. And the rest would go towards hiring and inventory.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: That's great.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I feel like there’s an opportunity here to kind of like build a whole campaign around like bra sizing is not fair, and, and things like that. It sounds like that’s your mission is to, like, make it culturally more okay and like help women feel more confident.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: And things like that. Are there, are there any other things that you’re doing to kind of push forward that mission besides just the product in front of me?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yes. So we’re doing a lot of fun things to have those type of conversations. For example, in March, it was National Pancake Day. And a lot of our customers mentioned when they were younger they got teased for having a pancake body. So we renamed it as National Flat Chest Day.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: We owned it and embraced it. So anyone who placed an order with us on that day, we sent them $4.65 back, which is exactly how much a short stack of pancakes costs at iHop. So it went viral in the press.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: That’s cool.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Our customers loved it.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I love this.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: And it was inexpensive. It was a really cheap way for us to get in front of the media, cut through noise. And it just, again, repositioned us as a brand that's not just making a bra, but we want to have these conversations.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Question for, for, Maia and Elizabeth more than, more than Charles.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: No offense taken.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Like I guess the price point, how do you think about it from a like quality of the product versus the price. Does it feel?

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: It feels fine to me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Yeah. It’s fine.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Like I think, so, there’s a, do you know Lively?

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: So I think Lively bras are probably $45.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: And they seem the same quality as these bras, which I think are also $45. Like, I think it's pretty standard.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: And is that the same price range as, like, Victoria’s Secret?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Um...

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I think Victoria’s Secret is probably more expensive.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: More expensive.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: But they’re like, they’re also much more, there’s like all kinds of bull***t hanging off.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: But for like a pretty everyday casual bra, this is like in line...

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I think standard.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Standard. Bras are a good market. That’s why you see all these bra companies.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I don't understand how challenging is it? Like I still cannot wrap my head around how hard is it to make a new bra for this audience?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: The thing I’m trying to wrap my head around, and this is me speaking from the perspective of probably squarely in your target demographic. What, what is different about these bras other than the size?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: For companies like, you know, take Third Love. Why is it that they cannot just extend into these cup sizes as well?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yeah. Most of these bra companies are already mass audience. They're trying to serve everyone. Um, and if you’re trying to serve everyone, there’s no way to develop the resources to be able to perfect the fit for all those sizes. For ours, we had to develop each, um, size, so that it perfectly fits that size, versus trying to use one single size and apply that design to every single person.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: But, but that is exactly, I think, I don't understand how challenging is it? Like I still cannot, even though I already asked you this, I cannot wrap my head around how hard is it to make a new bra for this audience?

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Well, and I'm, I’m comparing this to Lively, which I think is just, they're, they're like not really shaped bras. It's kind of, they're just, they're bralettes.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And Third Love is like a custom bra. And their messaging is also, like, we’re inclusive about everybody’s, you know, cup sizes or whatever you want to call it. Right. So you have people kind of going after this demographic. Not explicitly. Not building a brand around this.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Not, right, but.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: But they're in the space.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: So I've tried both of those bras, and they don't fit me. Um, so with Third Love, um, I still get the cup gap, they're still too deep, they're a little pointy on me. For Lively, because they're bralettes and they're not shaped, they don't really scoop me up. There's a bunching towards the cup. So, you know, even though they it's for all these different sizes, it wasn't made for those sizes.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: There is an opportunity here. I think I’m just trying to navigate...

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Are you worried that like Third Love is going to come in?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Competition. So competition's a big one. I think just in general, like, ecommerce scares me as a category because there are just so many additional challenges that pure software doesn't have. Right. Um, go-to-market is expensive, ecommerce has costs, although it sounds like your cost structure’s actually really good. And then these looming competitors, and I don’t understand, like, you know, I get that they haven’t cracked the nut, but if you start to do well, I’m pretty certain that other people will, will crack the nut. Like, I don’t believe this is rocket science. So this is like a first-mover, hustle advantage, which it sounds like you guys are doing well. So that, those are the things I’m thinking about.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: How big is this subset of the broader bra market?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yeah. We believe it to be a $5.1 billion market. And the way we got to this is the total lingerie market in the US is $16 billion. And around 32% of women fall in the BMI that would be applicable to us.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I'm just trying to figure out, if you can build a beachhead around this customer and you can speak to her and you're the person she goes to time and time again, like, how big is. The 5.1 number of the, it just feels bigger and it, I say this with all knowledge that I'm a man who doesn't wear a bra, that just feels like a larger chunk of the market than I was anticipating you saying. And if it's a smaller chunk that's not as well understood, I think there's an argument to be said that like it's just not worth it to specialize on this if it's not the only thing you do.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I mean, I don't know the data. But I would believe it. I would totally believe that.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I also believe in the market sizing, I mean, let's just take Asian Americans in this country, they're what, sub 20% of 300 million people and you spend 50 to 100 dollars in a bra, like there you go.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So. Um, and then I believe there are a lot of upsell opportunities for sure. Like, once you get that audience there are. So I’m not worried about that.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Yeah. I mean, the only way I know how you compete, I mean, because obviously Adore Me and those other folks have tons of cash. The only way you can really compete with them is to just play a different game, which is organic bottom-up community. So I like, like I buy that part. I’m still trying to in my mind sort out like, can you get big enough fast enough and own the category such that when those people do come, it’s like a futile effort?

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Right. That everyone’s like, No, no, no, like only Pepper does ...

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mhm. Yep.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: ... AA bras. Like you'd never get it from Adore Me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Right. You’re like first thought for this audience. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: So tell me, tell me more about, I mean you’ve run this really lean, tell me more about how you adjust to sort of having more resources and kind of what the plan is for how you’ll deploy them.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yes. So with this 1.5 million, it will go towards hiring, product development and continued growth. And most of it will be focused on growth. So paid acquisition we know is going to be a bigger part of this story. So we’re spending more resources there. With product development, we want to start developing strapless bras, our version of a pushup bra, even start thinking about swimsuits soon. And then the last part of it is community building and brand marketing. So right now with those initiatives like National Flat Chest Day, we can even bigger versions of that with more money. So we’re just waiting for the right resources.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: How do you sequence how much to bite off? I mean, you're still relatively early in kind of core bra. You've got sports bras, swimwear. How do you think about, how should I think about the sequencing of when you add new things versus sort of doubling and tripling down just on your core product today?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: The next two years will still be focused on bras. This is the number one pain point of our audience. Um, and the way women shop for bras is they need a bra depending on what they wear on top. So right now we only have the t-shirt bra, essentially. We still have so many different type of bras that we haven't conquered yet. So there's a lot of opportunity there. And after we, um, get the bra category is when we start thinking about things like swimsuit.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Where, where do you think investors can help you most?

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Yeah. I mean we’re first time founders. So we’re always open to advice from people who’ve done it before. And from done it before I mean have grown D2C businesses to successful exit, or have built really thriving communities, because that’s really important to us. One area we’re also diving into right now is wholesale. So we actually just launched a partnership with Urban Outfitters a few weeks ago, and that’s been met with really awesome response. They're placing a second purchase order now. So I think there’s opportunities to get in front of more women through these retail partnerships. But we want to make sure that we’re still maintaining that D2C essence, that community building essence of our brand as well.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Um, so I'm gonna pass on this opportunity. I think you're super bright, you know what you're doing. And you have seemingly decent unit economics. Um, I just, it's a category I know so little about that I'm just reluctant to, to invest in it. So for that, I'm gonna pass.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Thank you so much.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I think for me this is a pass. Personally kinda passionate about it. But all the things that we’ve discussed about the competitive landscape, I just anticipate a pretty rough path forward.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Thank you for the feedback.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: So look, here’s what I think. Um. I like you. I could be convinced that the market size is larger than my naive instincts suggest based on what some of my fellow panelists have said. So I’d like to make a small investment of $25k. I obviously have some diligence to do. But I’d love to work with you. I really value capital efficiency and um I also really value people who’ve picked a, a niche or a target customer that’s clearly defined and easy to identify. And it sounds to me like I really liked your answer about spending the next two years on bras. I think that’s your beachhead product and so defending that at all costs as a first step I think makes a lot of sense.

turns.speaker: Jaclyn
turns.text: Thank you. I can’t wait to work together.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I think you answered everything perfectly. And I love the hustle and the scrappiness. Of course, you've done a lot with very little. I also think that there is a big opportunity here. The valuation for me is really pricey, to be honest. Like this is where we come in with Hustle Fund. Um. For that reason I'm a pass. If you want to do revenue based financing, that is something we can potentially discuss.
